questions.stem: Which statement best describes ethics as a field of study?

options.text: A set of enforceable rules written by legislatures and interpreted by courts to govern practice
An individual's personal beliefs about right and wrong absorbed from family, culture, and faith
The customary courtesies and manners expected of members of a profession at work
The systematic study of right and wrong used to examine and justify standards of conduct

rationales.whyCorrect: Ethics is the disciplined, reasoned examination of moral judgments: it asks not only what people believe is right but what justifies calling an action right. Option B describes morals, which are personally held convictions rather than a method of analysis; option A describes law; option C describes etiquette. Keeping these apart matters clinically because a nurse may face a situation that is legal and perfectly polite yet still ethically questionable, and only ethical reasoning supplies language for that gap.
rationales.eli10: Everyone carries a private sense of what is fair — that private sense is your morals. Ethics is what happens when people stop simply feeling and start arguing: Is this fair? Why? Would it still be fair if the roles were reversed? Ethics is the reasoning and the justification, not the gut reaction. Law is what a government will actually enforce against you, and etiquette is polished behavior like introducing yourself before you touch someone. Four related ideas, four different jobs.

questions.stem: The framework commonly called principlism organizes biomedical ethical reasoning around which four principles?

options.text: Advocacy, accountability, collaboration, and delegation
Compassion, competence, confidence, and commitment
Respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice
Veracity, fidelity, confidentiality, and utility

rationales.whyCorrect: Principlism, associated with Beauchamp and Childress, structures bioethical analysis around four mid-level principles: respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. The other options list genuine professional concepts — veracity, fidelity, confidentiality, advocacy, accountability — but these operate as derivative rules, virtues, or role expectations rather than as the framework's core set. Learning the four as a set gives students a shared vocabulary before they study each one in depth.
rationales.eli10: Picture a four-legged stool you sit on whenever a health care decision gets hard. One leg is letting the person decide for themselves. One is actively doing good for them. questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the American Nurses Association Code of Ethics for Nurses?

options.text: To define the legal scope of nursing practice that each state board of nursing enforces
To express the profession's nonnegotiable moral standard: its values, obligations, and duties
To specify the exact steps a nurse must follow to resolve every ethical conflict
To list the disciplinary penalties imposed when a nurse commits a practice error

rationales.whyCorrect: The ANA describes the Code — revised in 2025 and now organized into ten provisions, each with interpretive statements — as a nonnegotiable moral standard for nurses in every setting and role. It states what nurses owe and why, but deliberately does not script how each obligation must be met in a given case. It is also not a statute: legal scope of practice comes from each state's nurse practice act, and disciplinary authority belongs to state boards of nursing. Recognizing the Code as a professional standard rather than law explains why it can demand more than the legal minimum.
rationales.eli10: A code of ethics is like the commitments a team writes and signs before the season: how we treat each other, what we will never do, who we intend to be. That is not the league rulebook that gets you ejected — the rulebook is the law, with referees and penalties. And the commitments do not tell you which play to call in the fourth quarter; they tell you what kind of team you promised to be while you figure the play out yourself.

questions.stem: Which comparison of deontology and utilitarianism is accurate?

options.text: Both evaluate an act solely by whether it produces the greatest benefit for the largest number of people
Deontology evaluates an act by its measurable outcomes, whereas utilitarianism evaluates it by the actor's underlying duties
Deontology evaluates an act by duties and rules, whereas utilitarianism evaluates it by its consequences for overall welfare
Both reject moral rules entirely and evaluate an act only by the character traits the actor displays

rationales.whyCorrect: Deontological (duty-based) theories hold that certain acts are right or wrong because of the obligation involved, independent of how the results turn out. Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory: rightness is judged by which option produces the greatest balance of benefit over harm across everyone affected. Option B reverses the two, option A collapses deontology into consequentialism, and option D describes virtue ethics. The contrast matters because the same case can yield opposite conclusions depending on which lens is applied.
rationales.eli10: Two teachers grade the same science project. The first only checks whether you followed the required procedure — correct method, full credit, no matter how the experiment turned out. That teacher is deontology, grading the duty. The second ignores your method and grades only the results and how useful they were. That is utilitarianism, grading the consequences. One project, two defensible grades — which is exactly why two people who both want to do right can reach opposite conclusions.

options.text: Which available option produces the greatest overall good for the greatest number?

Which principle should take priority when two ethical principles conflict?

questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between law and ethics in health care?

options.text: Any action that is legally permitted is, by that fact alone, also ethically acceptable
Law sets the highest expectation for conduct, and ethics applies only where no law exists
Ethical standards are enforced by the courts, while laws are enforced by professional associations
Legal and ethical standards overlap substantially, but an action can be legal and still be ethically troubling

rationales.whyCorrect: Law and ethics frequently reinforce one another, but they are distinct systems with different sources, scopes, and enforcement mechanisms. Law generally establishes an enforceable minimum, while professional ethics can demand more — the ANA Code, for instance, articulates obligations no statute compels. Option A commits the error of equating legality with morality, option C reverses the enforcement mechanisms, and option B wrongly confines ethics to the gaps left by legislation.
rationales.eli10: Think of a room. The law is the floor: you may not go below it, and if you do, someone with real authority stops you. Ethics is the ceiling, and it sits much higher. No statute requires you to explain a frightening test to a frightened patient gently rather than quickly, so you could do the legal minimum forever and never be sanctioned. But "I broke no rule" is a floor-level defense, and ethics asks you to stand up in the room, not merely stay off the ground.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures how the ethics of care differs from a principle-based approach such as principlism?

options.text: It applies universal rules uniformly so that every patient receives an identical response
It judges an action by which option produces the greatest net benefit across all affected
It emphasizes relationships, context, and responsiveness rather than the application of abstract principles
It ranks the four biomedical principles in a fixed order to be applied in every situation

rationales.whyCorrect: Care ethics, developed largely through theorists such as Gilligan and Noddings and influential in nursing, treats moral life as grounded in relationship and responsiveness to particular people rather than in impartial rules applied from a distance. It does not discard principles, but it insists that context, connection, and attentiveness carry genuine moral weight of their own. Options A and D describe rule- or principle-driven models, and option B states the utilitarian criterion rather than a relational one.
rationales.eli10: Two nurses hear the same anxious question from a patient. A rule-driven approach asks first, "What is the standard answer every patient should get?" — valuable, because it treats people equally and resists favoritism. Care ethics asks a different question first: who is this particular person, what does this moment mean to them, and what does the relationship between us require right now? It is not rule-breaking. It is the claim that the specifics of the person in front of you are moral information, not noise to filter out.

questions.stem: A public health agency compares two outbreak-response strategies and selects the one projected to prevent the largest total number of hospitalizations and deaths across the population. Which ethical theory is most clearly reflected in this reasoning?

options.text: Utilitarianism, because the option is chosen by the aggregate benefit it is expected to produce
Deontology, because the decision follows a duty that holds independently of the outcome
Virtue ethics, because the decision expresses the moral character of the officials involved
Care ethics, because the decision responds to particular relationships and individual context

rationales.whyCorrect: Choosing a strategy on the basis of projected total benefit across a population is classic consequentialist — specifically utilitarian — reasoning: rightness is determined by the balance of good over harm produced. A deontological approach would invoke a duty binding regardless of totals, virtue ethics would ask what a person of good character would do, and care ethics would foreground particular relationships and context. Naming the theory in use also makes its blind spots visible, since aggregate calculations can obscure how a strategy affects small or vulnerable groups.
rationales.eli10: Suppose a health department can fund exactly one of two campaigns and asks only one question: which one keeps more people out of the hospital? That is utilitarian reasoning — add up the expected good and take the bigger total. It is genuinely useful when you must decide for a whole population and cannot ask each person individually. It also carries a known catch: a bigger total can quietly conceal a group that received almost nothing, so naming the math is how you notice who was left out of the sum.

questions.stem: A hospital establishes a multidisciplinary clinical ethics committee. Which outcome is this structure primarily designed to produce?

options.text: Consultation, staff education, and policy review that support ethical decision making
Licensure discipline for clinicians whose judgment is questioned during a case review
Legally binding rulings that the treatment team is required to carry out as written
Transfer of decision-making authority away from the patient's family and care team

rationales.whyCorrect: Clinical ethics committees conventionally serve three overlapping functions: case consultation, education of staff and the wider institution, and development or review of organizational policy. Their recommendations are advisory rather than legally binding; they do not displace the patient, surrogate, or treatment team, and they hold no licensure authority, which rests with state boards of nursing and medicine. Understanding the committee as advisory helps students see it as a resource that widens deliberation rather than a tribunal that ends it.
rationales.eli10: An ethics committee is a group you bring a genuinely tangled situation to when you want more minds on it. They surface angles you missed, they teach, and they help rewrite institutional policies that keep generating the same conflict. What they are not is a principal handing out punishment or a judge issuing a verdict you must obey. You go for better thinking and a clearer set of options; the decision still belongs to the patient, the surrogate, and the team.

questions.stem: The Belmont Report was published after public revelations about the U.S. Public Health Service syphilis study at Tuskegee. Which statement best describes what the report contributed to healthcare ethics?

options.text: It enacted the first federal statute requiring that identifiable health information be kept confidential
It named three basic principles — respect for persons, beneficence, and justice — for human subjects research
It issued the first international code of research ethics, written in response to Nazi experimentation
It required every U.S. hospital to seat a standing ethics committee before it could treat patients

rationales.whyCorrect: The Belmont Report (1979), issued by a national commission and maintained by HHS, sets out three basic principles for research involving human subjects and ties each to a concrete application: respect for persons to informed consent, beneficence to risk–benefit assessment, and justice to fair selection of subjects. It is a foundational ethics document, not a statute — federal health privacy protections came later through HIPAA, and the postwar Nuremberg Code, not Belmont, was the first international research code. Its history shows how documented abuses reshaped the ethical framework of health care.
rationales.eli10: Some safety rules only get written after something has already gone badly wrong. After decades in which researchers deceived Black men in Alabama and withheld treatment in order to study untreated syphilis, the country wrote down three ground rules for studying human beings: treat people as people who get to decide, weigh risks against benefits honestly, and choose participants fairly instead of choosing whoever is easiest to enroll. That is the Belmont Report — a lesson recorded so it would not have to be learned again.

questions.stem: Which comparison of descriptive ethics and normative ethics is accurate?

options.text: Descriptive ethics prescribes which actions are obligatory, while normative ethics reports the beliefs people hold
Descriptive ethics reports what people actually believe and do, while normative ethics argues what ought to be done
Descriptive ethics applies only to individual clinicians, while normative ethics applies only to institutions
Both are empirical fields, since each measures the moral beliefs a group actually holds at a given time

rationales.whyCorrect: Descriptive ethics is empirical: it studies, through survey and observation, the moral beliefs and behaviors that actually exist in a group. Normative ethics is prescriptive: it constructs and defends arguments about what people are obligated to do. Option A reverses the definitions, option D misclassifies normative ethics as empirical, and option C invents a distinction by level of analysis that neither branch draws. The real distinction guards against a common reasoning error — treating the finding that most clinicians do something as proof that doing it is right.
rationales.eli10: A weather report tells you it is raining. It does not tell you to carry an umbrella — that is a separate step where someone gives advice and can be asked to justify it. Descriptive ethics is the weather report: here is what people in this group actually believe and actually do, measured. Normative ethics is the advice plus the argument behind it. Collapsing the two produces the classic mistake of thinking "everybody does it around here" settles whether it is right.

questions.stem: A student asserts that once an ethical principle clearly applies to a case, it can never be outweighed by any other consideration. Which response best reflects how principlism actually treats its principles?

options.text: Principles are prima facie binding: each holds unless, in this case, a competing obligation is weightier
Principles are absolute, so any apparent conflict between two of them means one was misidentified
Principles are optional ideals, so a clinician may set any of them aside based on personal preference
Principles are permanently ranked, so the same principle resolves every conflict in the same direction

rationales.whyCorrect: In principlism the four principles are prima facie rather than absolute: each is genuinely binding and may be overridden only when a competing obligation carries greater weight in the specific circumstances, and the override itself must be justified. Resolution therefore proceeds by specification (making a principle concrete for the case at hand) and balancing (weighing conflicting obligations with reasons), not by consulting a fixed hierarchy. Options B and D would make real conflict either impossible or mechanical, and option C mistakes a justified override for personal discretion, which the framework explicitly rules out.
rationales.eli10: Suppose you promised a friend you would attend their game Saturday and also promised your grandmother you would help her move that same Saturday. Both promises are real; neither became fake just because they collided. You have to weigh them, choose, and be able to explain the choice — and the promise you set aside still leaves a residue, such as an apology or a make-up date you now owe. That is what prima facie means: binding on its face, overridable only for a genuinely stronger reason, never by a shrug.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines the ethical principle of autonomy as it is used in healthcare?

options.text: Distributing limited healthcare resources fairly among all the patients who need them
Respecting a capable person's right to make informed decisions about their own care
Choosing the course of action that produces the greatest overall benefit for the patient
Keeping promises and honoring the commitments the clinician has made to the patient

rationales.whyCorrect: Autonomy (literally 'self-rule') holds that a person with decision-making capacity has the right to govern what is done to their own body, free from controlling interference, once they have the information needed to choose. The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses, Provision 1.4, frames this as the moral and legal right to determine what will be done with and to one's own person. The other options name distinct principles: fair distribution is justice, maximizing benefit is beneficence, and honoring commitments is fidelity. The distinction matters because clinicians frequently defend an action as 'good for the patient' when the value actually at stake is the patient's own self-determination.
rationales.eli10: Autonomy comes from Greek roots meaning 'self' and 'rule' — you are the one who governs you. Two things have to be true for it to be real: you have to know what your options actually are, and the final call has to be yours. A clinician can describe every door in the house and say which one they would walk through, but they cannot take the key. Fairness, doing good, and keeping promises are all genuine obligations too — they just have their own names and their own logic.

questions.stem: Which term describes overriding the decision of a patient who has decision-making capacity because a clinician believes a different choice would be better for that patient?

options.text: Advocacy

options.text: The right to refuse a recommended treatment even when the care team disagrees
The right to receive the same standard of care given to other patients on the unit

questions.stem: Which comparison of decision-making capacity and competence is accurate?

options.text: Capacity is a legal status determined by a court, while competence is a clinical judgment made at the bedside

rationales.eli10: Compare holding a driver's license with being fit to drive this car on this road right now. questions.stem: When a patient loses decision-making capacity and a surrogate must decide, which standard best preserves the patient's autonomy?

options.text: The best-interest standard, choosing what most clinicians would recommend for a patient in this condition
The surrogate's own values and preferences, since the patient can no longer state an objection to them
Substituted judgment, choosing what the patient would have chosen based on previously expressed wishes and values
The preference held by the majority of the family members who are present at the bedside

rationales.whyCorrect: Substituted judgment carries autonomy past the loss of capacity by asking what this specific patient would have decided, drawing on advance directives, prior statements, and known values; ANA Provision 1.4 directs alternate decision-makers to rely on the patient's previously expressed wishes and known values. The best-interest standard is the fallback used only when those wishes are genuinely unknown, and it expresses beneficence rather than self-determination. Substituting the surrogate's own preferences or taking a family vote replaces the patient's voice instead of transmitting it, which is why neither is an autonomy-preserving standard.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a friend steps out and leaves you to place her order. You do not order what you like, and you do not poll the table — you order what she would have ordered, because you remember she cannot stand olives. That is substituted judgment: the surrogate acts as a messenger for a voice that is temporarily missing, not as a replacement for it. Only when no one has any idea what she would want do you fall back on what is generally good for someone in her situation.

questions.stem: Under which circumstance is limiting an individual patient's autonomy most ethically defensible?

options.text: When the patient's family strongly disagrees with the decision the patient has made
When the patient's choice differs from the treatment the interprofessional team recommends
When the patient's choice creates a substantial risk of serious harm to other people
When the patient's choice is likely to result in serious harm to the patient personally

questions.stem: A hospitalized adult with full decision-making capacity tells the nurse, "In my family, my oldest son and I decide these things together, and I want him told first." Which interpretation of this request is most accurate?

options.text: The request must be declined, because autonomy requires that patients make treatment decisions individually
The request is an exercise of autonomy, because choosing how and with whom to decide is self-determination
The request suggests impaired decision-making capacity and should trigger a formal capacity evaluation
The request converts the situation into surrogate decision-making, which requires legal documentation first

questions.stem: Which example best demonstrates a nurse acting to support patient autonomy?

options.text: Leaving out the option the team considers clearly inferior so the patient is not tempted to select it
Repeating the team's recommendation at every interaction until the patient agrees to the recommended plan
Asking the patient's adult child to make the choice because the treatment options are complicated
Explaining the implications of each reasonable option and then honoring a choice the team did not recommend

rationales.whyCorrect: Supporting autonomy means confirming the patient's understanding, presenting all reasonable options with their implications, and then acting on the resulting choice (D) — the obligation ANA Provision 1.4 assigns to nurses, which explicitly covers accepting, refusing, or terminating treatment without deceit, undue influence, duress, or coercion. Voluntariness is as essential as information: omitting an option the team dislikes (A) is controlling influence disguised as guidance, because it manipulates the choice set rather than the patient's reasoning and the patient never learns a choice existed; repeated pressure (B) erodes voluntariness and shades from persuasion into coercion; and handing a capable patient's decision to a relative (C) removes the decision from the person entitled to make it, since complexity calls for better explanation, not a substitute decision maker. Autonomy is respected in the follow-through, not merely in the opening conversation.
rationales.eli10: Supporting a choice is like being a good map, not a leash. A complete map shows every road and marks honestly which ones have potholes, then lets the driver pick the route. Nagging until they turn, handing the wheel to their child, or quietly erasing a road from the map all end with someone else driving — and the erased road is the sneakiest, because the driver never knows a choice was taken. The nurse's job is to make the map complete and understood, then stay in the car even if the driver picks the bumpy road.

questions.stem: An older adult with early-stage dementia clearly states which medications he wants to keep taking and why, but cannot describe the implications of a proposed major surgery even after repeated explanation. Which approach best reflects respect for autonomy?

options.text: Route all future healthcare decisions to a surrogate, since the dementia diagnosis establishes loss of capacity
Honor his own decisions in the areas he demonstrably understands and involve a surrogate only for the surgery
Document his stated preferences but delay acting on any of them until his capacity is formally restored
Seek a court ruling of incompetence so that one decision-maker can be appointed for every aspect of care

rationales.whyCorrect: Capacity is decision-specific and sliding-scale: a patient may meet the threshold for a familiar, low-complexity decision while falling short for a high-stakes one that requires appreciating complex risks and alternatives. Options A, D, and C treat capacity as an all-or-nothing switch and strip the patient of choices he demonstrably can still make.
rationales.eli10: Capacity is not one master switch that is either on or off; it is a row of switches, one per decision. This man can still reach the switch labeled 'which of my daily pills do I want,' because he understands those and can explain his reasoning. The switch labeled 'major surgery' is out of reach today, so someone helps with that one only. Taking his hand off every switch because one is stuck is not protection — it is a larger loss than the situation calls for.

questions.stem: An adult with decision-making capacity is admitted to a hospital that participates in Medicare, is given information about advance directives, and declines to complete one. Under the federal Patient Self-Determination Act, what must the facility do?

options.text: Require a completed advance directive before any elective procedure may be scheduled for him
Appoint a surrogate decision-maker now, because no advance directive is on file for him
Document that no directive exists and continue his care without discriminating on that basis
Apply a federally standardized default directive to his record until he signs one of his own

questions.stem: A patient with intact decision-making capacity insists on receiving an intervention that the care team has concluded is not medically indicated for his condition. Which statement best describes the scope of the autonomy-based right at issue?

options.text: Autonomy protects a capable patient's refusal of offered care but does not compel provision of non-indicated care
Autonomy no longer applies here, because a request outside clinical indications signals impaired capacity
Autonomy requires the team to provide the requested intervention, because the patient has decision-making capacity
Autonomy obligates the team to comply unless a written hospital policy specifically prohibits the intervention

rationales.whyCorrect: Autonomy functions chiefly as a negative right — a right against unwanted intrusion on one's body — so it grounds a strong claim to decline what is offered but not a positive claim that obligates clinicians to deliver whatever is requested. Option B mistakes disagreement for incapacity, which is the most common misuse of capacity assessment, and option D treats organizational policy as the only boundary when professional standards and the principle itself already set one. The autonomy-respecting response is to explore the goals behind the request, explain why the intervention is not offered, and present the alternatives that are.
rationales.eli10: There is a real difference between 'no one can make me' and 'I can make you.' Autonomy is the first kind of claim: nothing goes into your body without your agreement. It is not a vending machine in which every button pressed must be dispensed, because the clinician's professional judgment is part of the transaction rather than an obstacle to it. Saying 'we won't do that, here is why, and here is what we can do' does not overrule the patient's choice — it describes what was on offer to choose from.

questions.stem: A patient with intact decision-making capacity declines a recommended treatment after clearly describing the likely consequences. Which nursing action best respects autonomy without crossing into abandonment?

options.text: Document the refusal, continue supportive care, and remain available if the patient's condition or goals change
Document the refusal and end all further discussion of the topic, since revisiting it would be coercive
Ask the provider to seek a court order authorizing the treatment over the capable patient's objection
Limit contact to required tasks so that the patient does not feel pressured to reconsider the refusal

rationales.whyCorrect: Respecting a refusal ends the pressure, not the relationship: symptom management, supportive care, and open communication continue, and the decision may appropriately be revisited when clinical circumstances or the patient's own stated goals change, which is offering information rather than applying pressure. Withdrawing engagement (B and D) mistakes autonomy for indifference, leaves the patient without care they have not refused, and can constitute abandonment. Seeking a court order against a patient with capacity (C) is paternalism escalated through the legal system and misuses a process meant for patients who lack capacity. Autonomy is best honored when a patient's refusal costs them nothing in care or in relationship.
rationales.eli10: 'That is your call' and 'then I am done with you' are not the same sentence, though they are easy to blur in practice. Think of a coach whose athlete refuses one drill: the coach stops pushing, keeps working with her on everything else, and stays on the deck. Backing off the pressure while staying present is what accepting a refusal looks like. Quietly reducing contact reads as punishment even when it is meant as respect — and the patient still needs the care they never declined.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines the ethical principle of nonmaleficence?

options.text: The duty to refrain from inflicting harm and to avoid exposing patients to risk that is not justified
The duty to distribute limited benefits, resources, and burdens fairly among the patients being served
The duty to actively promote a patient's well-being and to remove conditions that are harming the patient
The duty to honor commitments made to a patient and to remain faithful to that professional relationship

rationales.whyCorrect: In the four-principles framework used across bioethics and nursing ethics, nonmaleficence is the obligation not to inflict harm and not to impose risks that lack a proportionate expected benefit. It is stated as a negative, or restraining, duty: it is satisfied by not doing certain things, and it is breached both by causing injury and by needlessly exposing a patient to the possibility of injury. The distractors define three different principles: justice, the fair distribution of benefits and burdens (B); beneficence, the positive duty to promote welfare and remove harmful conditions (C); and fidelity, faithfulness to commitments made within the professional relationship (D). Each is a separate obligation with distinct content, and none of them is the duty to avoid inflicting harm.
rationales.eli10: Two different promises sit at the center of clinical care. One is "I will act to make you better." The other is "I will not injure you, and I will not gamble with you for no reason." Nonmaleficence is the second promise, and notice that it covers risk, not just actual damage. A nurse who gives a drug without checking the allergy list has breached it even if nothing bad happens, because the patient was put in danger that no expected benefit justified. That is why the principle is the floor everything else is built on.

questions.stem: The phrase primum non nocere ("first, do no harm") is most directly an expression of which idea?

options.text: That clinicians are obligated to provide whatever intervention a patient or family requests
That aggregate benefit to a community can outweigh serious risk borne by one patient
That patients themselves carry final responsibility for the outcomes of their treatment
That avoiding and minimizing harm is a baseline obligation present in all patient care

rationales.whyCorrect: Primum non nocere is the traditional Latin formulation of nonmaleficence, marking the avoidance of harm as a minimum standing obligation rather than an optional goal. It does not require that care be risk-free, which would make most treatment impossible; it requires that risk be minimized and justified by expected benefit. The other options each misdescribe the principle: option A misstates autonomy as a duty to comply with any request, when respecting autonomy grants a patient the right to refuse rather than a right to demand nonbeneficial treatment; option B states a utilitarian trade-off that nonmaleficence specifically resists, since aggregate benefit does not license imposing serious unjustified risk on an individual patient; and option C shifts professional responsibility onto the patient, when the duty to avoid harm rests with the clinician.
rationales.eli10: Read the phrase carefully: it says "first," not "only." It is a rule about sequence, not a ban on action. Before you ask whether an intervention will help, you ask what it could cost the patient and whether that cost is defensible. It also does not license paralysis, because withholding needed care is itself a way of harming someone. The instruction is to make harm the first item you evaluate in every plan, every time, and to keep evaluating it as the plan changes.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates beneficence rather than one of the other core ethical principles?

options.text: A nurse teaches a newly diagnosed patient to use a glucose meter so he can manage diabetes at home
A nurse holds a scheduled dose after noting that the patient's heart rate has dropped sharply
A nurse documents a patient's refusal of a treatment and notifies the prescribing clinician promptly
A nurse assigns limited clinic appointment slots by medical urgency rather than by type of insurance

rationales.whyCorrect: Beneficence is a positive duty: the clinician takes action that actively contributes to the patient's welfare rather than merely avoiding injury. Teaching self-monitoring adds a capability the patient did not previously have and improves expected long-term outcomes, which is benefit conferred rather than harm averted. Option B is nonmaleficence expressed as restraint, option C reflects respect for autonomy, and option D reflects distributive justice.
rationales.eli10: Sort clinical actions by what would happen if the nurse did nothing. If the answer is "something bad occurs," the action was preventing harm. If the answer is "nothing bad occurs, the patient just stays where he was," the action was adding benefit. Nobody is in danger the moment a glucose meter lesson begins; the patient simply ends up more capable than he started. That forward push toward a better state, not a rescue from a worse one, is what beneficence names.

questions.stem: Which comparison of beneficence and nonmaleficence is accurate?

options.text: Beneficence binds physicians alone, whereas nonmaleficence binds every member of the care team
Beneficence governs routine bedside care, whereas nonmaleficence governs research and experimental therapy
Beneficence is a positive duty to act for the patient's good; nonmaleficence is a duty to refrain from harm
Beneficence is codified in state statute, whereas nonmaleficence is an ideal with no practical force

rationales.whyCorrect: The structural difference between the principles is the direction of the obligation: beneficence requires performing acts that benefit the patient, while nonmaleficence requires not performing acts that injure the patient. Because a duty of restraint is owed continuously and impartially while a duty to act must be limited by feasibility and role, nonmaleficence is often, though not invariably, treated as the more stringent obligation when the two collide; Beauchamp and Childress caution against treating that ordering as an automatic rule. Both principles bind all clinicians in both clinical and research settings, and both are ethical obligations rather than statutes.
rationales.eli10: Compare two household rules: "cook dinner" and "do not set the kitchen on fire." The second is owed at every moment and to everyone, and you can satisfy it while asleep. The first takes effort, resources, and judgment about when and for whom, so it necessarily has limits. That asymmetry explains why the duty not to harm usually carries more weight in a conflict. It does not make beneficence optional, but it does mean a plan that helps somewhat while injuring seriously is normally rejected.

questions.stem: In the Belmont Report, which frames the ethical conduct of human-subjects research, how is the obligation to avoid harm treated?

options.text: It is omitted, because research risk is governed by federal regulation rather than by ethical principle
It replaces beneficence, since research is designed to produce knowledge rather than benefit participants
It is listed as a separate fourth principle applying only to studies that enroll vulnerable populations
It is folded into beneficence, stated as two rules: do not harm, and maximize benefits while minimizing harms

rationales.whyCorrect: The Belmont Report names three basic principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. It expresses beneficence through two general rules, quoted directly as "(1) do not harm and (2) maximize possible benefits and minimize possible harms." Nonmaleficence is therefore contained within beneficence in that framework rather than named separately, unlike the four-principles model that treats them as distinct obligations. Recognizing the difference keeps students from assuming that every ethics framework partitions principles identically, and from concluding that a three-principle framework has ignored harm.
rationales.eli10: Two maps of the same city can draw the district lines differently without disagreeing about where the streets are. The four-principles model draws "do good" and "do no harm" as two neighboring districts. Belmont draws one district called beneficence containing both instructions. Nothing about the underlying obligation changed. The practical lesson is to read what a framework says rather than counting its headings, because the same duty can appear under different labels depending on who is drawing the map.

questions.stem: A hospice patient's pain is uncontrolled, and the team titrates opioid therapy upward while accepting a foreseen risk of sedation and respiratory depression. Which ethical reasoning best supports this decision?

questions.stem: What is most likely to result when a clinician acts on beneficence while disregarding what the patient values and wants?

questions.stem: Which organizational change would most directly strengthen nonmaleficence in day-to-day clinical practice?

questions.stem: Nonmaleficence is usually stated as a duty to refrain from harmful acts. Which situation best shows that the duty can also be breached by failing to act?

questions.stem: An older adult at high risk for falls becomes restless and repeatedly tries to get out of bed at night. Which plan best balances beneficence and nonmaleficence?

options.text: Apply a vest restraint at bedtime so that the patient cannot get out of bed without assistance
Document the fall risk and take no further action, since any intervention introduces some new risk
Lower the bed, offer scheduled toileting, and round purposefully, reserving restraints for when these fail
Give a sedating medication nightly so the patient sleeps through the highest-risk overnight hours

rationales.whyCorrect: The least restrictive effective plan delivers the intended benefit of fall prevention while minimizing the harms restraints carry, including deconditioning, delirium, skin and nerve injury, and psychological distress. Nightly sedation is the same trade wearing different packaging, since it raises the very fall risk it was meant to lower. So you start with the measures whose cost is near zero, escalate only if they genuinely fail, and remember that inaction is not the neutral option, because the fall you did not try to prevent is also on your ledger.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why nearly every beneficent intervention must still be evaluated under nonmaleficence?

options.text: Because beneficence is an optional ideal, while nonmaleficence is the only duty binding on clinicians

Because nonmaleficence governs omissions, while beneficence governs only the acts actually performed
Because patient harm arises only when a clinician departs from a written policy of the organization

rationales.eli10: Benefit and risk arrive attached to each other, which is why a package insert lists indications and adverse effects on the same page. Doing good and avoiding harm are not two boxes to tick in sequence; they are one judgment made on a scale.

questions.stem: Which comparison accurately distinguishes nonmaleficence from negligence?

options.text: Nonmaleficence addresses intentional harm alone; negligence covers every accidental or unforeseen harm a patient experiences
Nonmaleficence is an ethical duty to avoid harm; negligence is a legal finding requiring duty, breach, causation, and damages
Nonmaleficence is defined by state nurse practice acts; negligence is defined by professional codes of ethics and standards
Nonmaleficence and negligence are interchangeable terms, since each names a failure to prevent injury to a patient

rationales.whyCorrect: Nonmaleficence is a normative ethical principle expressed in professional codes such as the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses, whereas negligence is a civil legal conclusion reached only when a duty of care existed, was breached, and that breach proximately caused compensable damages. Conduct can fall short of nonmaleficence without satisfying those elements, as with a near-miss that injures no one, and conversely an organizational policy can be followed exactly while the ethical duty is still unmet. rationales.eli10: Ethics and civil law overlap but are not the same instrument, and they have different entry requirements. Negligence is a finding in a civil suit, and it does not exist without proof of all four elements, including actual damages, so a dangerous error caught before it reaches the patient produces no negligence claim at all. The ethical duty is already engaged at that point, because the patient was exposed to unjustified risk. That gap is the whole point: the law sets a floor for liability, while nonmaleficence sets a standard you are answerable to even when no one was hurt and no one sues.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the ethical principle of justice as it is used in healthcare ethics?

options.text: Distributing benefits, burdens, and resources fairly and without arbitrary discrimination
Acting in ways that actively promote a patient's overall well-being and best interests
Honoring a competent patient's right to make informed decisions about their own care
Avoiding actions that inflict unnecessary harm or expose patients to undue risk

rationales.eli10: One pizza, a table of hungry people. 'Make sure this kid gets fed' is a question about one person. It is the fairness-of-the-slices principle, and its core rule is that a smaller slice needs a reason that actually relates to the situation — not someone's accent, job, or bank balance. Any time you find yourself comparing how two patients were treated, you have moved into justice territory.

questions.stem: The formal principle of justice, traced to Aristotle, is most accurately stated as which of the following?

options.text: Every person should receive an identical quantity of each healthcare resource available
Resources should flow to whoever is both able and willing to pay the market price
Resources should be distributed so that total benefit to the whole population is maximized

Give larger shoes to whoever's family donated money and it collapses, because money has nothing to do with feet. That is the whole formal principle — and notice it never tells you which differences count. That blank is exactly what the arguments over need versus benefit versus waiting time are trying to fill.

questions.stem: Which comparison of equality and equity in health care is accurate?

options.text: Equality adjusts what each group receives to match its baseline needs, while equity gives everyone an identical intervention
Equality and equity are interchangeable terms, since both require that every patient receive exactly the same treatment
Equality governs only population-level public health programs, while equity governs only individual decisions at the bedside

Option A simply reverses the two definitions, and equal inputs can actually widen outcome gaps when baseline needs differ substantially.
rationales.eli10: Three people of different heights watch a game over a fence. Equality hands all three the same box, so the shortest still sees nothing. Completion of a signed form, a witness signature, and filing of that form in the patient's permanent medical record

questions.stem: Which comparison of express consent and implied consent is accurate?

options.text: Express consent must always be in writing, whereas implied consent is any agreement the patient communicates aloud to the clinician

questions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes decision-making capacity from competence?

options.text: The terms are interchangeable in practice, and a patient is considered to lack either one only after a court has issued a ruling
Capacity, once lost, is considered permanent, whereas competence fluctuates along with the patient's clinical condition day to day
Capacity is a clinical judgment about one specific decision at one point in time, whereas competence is a legal determination made by a court
Capacity may be judged by any member of the care team, whereas competence must be certified by a consulting psychiatrist before care proceeds

Option D misstates authority: capacity assessment is a clinical determination made by the responsible clinician, not a psychiatric certification, and competence is never established by a consultant.
rationales.eli10: The two words answer different questions asked by different institutions. The legal question is broad and durable: does this person retain general authority over their own affairs? questions.stem: A surgeon closes every consent discussion by asking, "Do you have any questions?" Which change to this practice would most likely strengthen the validity of the consent obtained?

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates the emergency exception to informed consent?

options.text: An adult child signs the consent form for a capable patient because the patient reads slowly and the operating room team is waiting
A patient with intact capacity refuses a blood transfusion, and the team proceeds anyway because the refusal appears medically unwise

questions.stem: A hospitalized adult speaks only Vietnamese. The surgeon explains an upcoming procedure in English while the patient's teenage nephew interprets, and the patient then signs the consent form. Which element of informed consent is most directly compromised?

questions.stem: A patient who signed a consent form for a diagnostic bronchoscopy says in the pre-procedure area, "I've changed my mind — I don't want this done." Which statement most accurately reflects informed consent principles?

The withdrawal takes effect only if the patient documents the change of mind in writing before leaving the unit

Consent is revocable, so a patient with capacity may withdraw it at any time and the team should stop the process

questions.stem: Under the U.S. Common Rule governing research with human subjects (45 CFR 46.116), which requirement applies to informed consent for research participation?

Health information stored in a hospital's electronic health record, but not the same information on paper or in speech

questions.stem: Which statement accurately describes how a just culture matches its response to different categories of unsafe acts?

Review the facility's skills reference for the procedure and then perform it without assistance
Inform the charge nurse that she has not been trained and request supervised instruction first
Perform the procedure and document afterward that this was her first attempt at the skill

rationales.whyCorrect: Accountability requires an honest appraisal of one's own competence and an obligation to decline to act beyond it until competence is established; a nurse who performs an unfamiliar procedure remains answerable for the outcome regardless of who issued the assignment. Requesting supervised instruction meets the patient-care need while keeping the patient safe, and it activates the organization's orientation and competency-validation process so the nurse can perform the skill independently afterward. Reading a reference does not substitute for demonstrated competence on a hands-on skill, and documenting inexperience after the fact does not retroactively make an unsafe act safe; it only records that the unsafe act occurred.
rationales.eli10: The instinct is to treat asking for help as an admission of weakness, and it is worth seeing why that instinct runs backwards. Simply refusing the assignment would accomplish only the first. The piece students most often miss is that an assignment does not transfer the outcome upward. questions.stem: A nurse discovers that she administered a scheduled medication to the wrong patient, who currently shows no signs of harm. Which set of actions best reflects professional accountability?

options.text: Assess the patient, notify the prescriber, chart the drug given and the response, and file an occurrence report
Record the event only on the occurrence report so that the medical record does not show that an error occurred
Monitor the patient and, if no effects appear by end of shift, treat the event as a near miss that needs no report
Notify the prescriber only if symptoms develop, since reporting policies apply to events that cause actual harm

The medical record documents the objective clinical facts; the occurrence report is a separate administrative document that is not referenced in the chart, but that separation never justifies omitting the administration from the record. This event is also not a near miss — a near miss is an error intercepted before it reaches the patient, and this drug reached one. Waiting for harm to appear before acting substitutes luck for judgment and removes the event from the data the organization needs.
rationales.eli10: Order matters more here than students expect. questions.stem: Which example best illustrates at-risk behavior rather than human error or reckless behavior?

options.text: A nurse reads the label carefully but selects a look-alike vial stored beside the intended drug
A nurse charts vital signs from memory after finishing rounds, believing the shortcut is harmless
A nurse withdraws a controlled substance without an order and falsifies the administration record
A nurse overrides a smart pump's dose limit after a formal directive not to bypass the safeguard

rationales.whyCorrect: At-risk behavior is a behavioral drift in which a person makes a choice that raises risk while not perceiving that risk, or while believing the shortcut is justified; the defining feature is unrecognized or rationalized hazard, and the appropriate response is coaching plus removal of whatever incentive produced the drift. Option A is human error: the correct process was followed and an unintended slip occurred, driven substantially by a system hazard in how the vials were stored. Options C and D are reckless behavior, because in each the risk has already been made explicit and is consciously disregarded, which warrants disciplinary action even if no patient is harmed.
rationales.eli10: The category is usually settled by what the person believed at the moment they acted. 'I did not mean to do that' points to human error. 'I always do it this way and nothing has ever gone wrong' points to at-risk behavior — the person is not being defiant, they have simply stopped seeing the hazard, often because the shortcut saves time and has never yet cost anything. 'I was told plainly this was dangerous and I did it anyway' points to reckless behavior. The middle category is the one most often misclassified, and the tell is a sincere belief that the shortcut is fine. Once someone has been told directly and continues, that belief is no longer available as an explanation.

questions.stem: During shift report a nurse observes that a colleague assigned to patient care smells strongly of alcohol, has slurred speech, and is unsteady. Which response best fulfills the observing nurse's professional accountability?

options.text: Offer to absorb the colleague's patient assignment so that the situation does not draw attention

Wait until a second, similar occurrence establishes a clear pattern before reporting anything
Report the observation to the supervisor immediately so the colleague is removed from patient care

questions.stem: What would most likely result if nursing relied solely on external regulation — licensure law and employer policy — with no internal professional self-regulation?

options.text: Practice standards would rise, because legal penalties motivate conduct more reliably than ethical commitment
Nursing would still satisfy the definition of a profession, since professions are defined by licensure alone
Conduct would be held only to the enforceable legal minimum, leaving many ethical obligations unaddressed
Accountability would be unchanged, because law and professional ethics impose essentially identical obligations

rationales.whyCorrect: Law and organizational policy define a floor of acceptable conduct, and that floor is deliberately narrow because each element must be specific enough to prove and enforce. A large share of professional obligation is invisible to external enforcement: maintaining competence between renewal cycles, disclosing an error no one else witnessed, coaching a colleague's unsafe habit, declining a task beyond one's competence. Internal self-regulation — expressed in the ANA Code of Ethics and reinforced by peer expectation and personal standards — is what holds practice above that floor. Option B also inverts an important relationship, since a profession is characterized by self-governance over its own standards rather than by licensure alone, and licensure itself derives from statute rather than from the Code.
rationales.eli10: A useful way to test this claim is to ask what an outside enforcer can actually detect. It can detect a falsified record, an expired license, a diverted narcotic. If fear of being caught were the only motivation in play, everything undetectable would quietly erode — and a great deal of nursing is undetectable. That is the practical reason professions govern themselves from the inside: external rules only ever reach the bottom of the behavior, never the top.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes what makes a situation a true ethical dilemma?

options.text: Two or more defensible ethical obligations conflict, so honoring one means the other cannot be fully honored
The clinically correct action is unclear because key diagnostic or historical information has not yet been gathered
A clinician is certain which action is right, but an external constraint prevents them from carrying it out
A proposed course of action plainly violates statute, so the legally permissible option is already settled

rationales.whyCorrect: An ethical dilemma exists when genuinely competing goods or duties are each supported by legitimate ethical reasoning and no available option satisfies all of them at once. This is categorically different from a knowledge gap (a factual or clinical question), from a constrained-action problem (moral distress, per AACN and the ANA 2025 Code glossary), and from a settled legal question. Naming the situation accurately matters because dilemmas call for structured deliberation among stakeholders, whereas the other three call for data gathering, removal of the constraint, or application of an existing rule.
rationales.eli10: The word dilemma gets used loosely for anything hard, but in ethics it means something specific: both options have real ethical weight behind them, and choosing one costs you the other. Compare that to three situations people confuse it with. If you just need more information, that is a puzzle, and more data solves it. If you already know the right move but something is blocking you, that is a different problem with a different fix. If the law already answers it, there was never a live choice. Only the genuine collision of two legitimate duties requires the kind of deliberation ethics offers.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of patient advocacy in professional nursing practice?

options.text: To persuade reluctant patients to accept the plan of care the healthcare team has already recommended
To explain and defend institutional policy so that patients understand the limits placed on their choices
To protect and promote the rights, health, safety, and expressed interests of the person receiving care
To assume decision-making responsibility for patients who appear overwhelmed by the options presented

rationales.whyCorrect: Provision 3 of the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses (2025 edition) states that the nurse establishes a trusting relationship and advocates for the rights, health, and safety of recipients of nursing care, with interpretive statement 3.2 devoted specifically to advocating for those persons. Advocacy amplifies the patient's own voice and interests within the system rather than substituting the clinician's or the institution's preferences for them. That is why persuasion toward a predetermined outcome, defense of policy, and taking over the decision all fall outside the advocacy role, even when each is offered in good faith.
rationales.eli10: Advocacy is often misread as one of two things it is not: talking the patient into the recommended plan, or taking the decision off their hands. Both replace the patient's voice with someone else's. The actual function is closer to interpretation and amplification. The healthcare system moves fast, uses its own vocabulary, and has a steep authority gradient, so a patient's concern can be raised and still not land. The advocate makes sure it lands, and makes sure the version that lands is the patient's version, not a cleaned-up one that happens to agree with the team.

questions.stem: The American Association of Critical-Care Nurses defines moral distress as occurring when a clinician:

options.text: Believes they know, or is uncertain of, the ethically correct action but is constrained from taking it
Feels emotionally depleted after prolonged exposure to the suffering and loss of patients in their care
Disagrees with a colleague about which of two clinically reasonable treatment options is likely to work better
Experiences declining job satisfaction after repeated schedule changes, short staffing, and heavy assignments

rationales.whyCorrect: AACN states that moral distress occurs when a clinician believes they know, or is uncertain of, the ethically correct action and is constrained from taking it; the ANA 2025 Code glossary similarly ties moral distress to being unable to act because of constraints beyond one's individual control. Constraints may be institutional, hierarchical, legal, or resource-based, which is why effective remedies target the constraint rather than only the individual's coping capacity.
rationales.eli10: Moral distress has a precise definition worth holding onto, because it is routinely mislabeled as burnout. Something outside you stands between you and the action your professional judgment points toward. Notice that AACN's definition deliberately covers uncertainty too, so you can be genuinely unsure what is right and still be morally distressed by being unable to pursue the question. Because the source of the problem sits outside the individual, individual coping strategies alone will not resolve it.

questions.stem: Which comparison between an ethical dilemma and moral distress is accurate?

options.text: Both involve uncertainty about the right action, but only a dilemma carries emotional consequences for the clinician
A dilemma is experienced by individuals, while moral distress is a property of institutions rather than of people
Moral distress always precedes a decision, whereas a dilemma is recognizable only after the outcome is known
A dilemma concerns which duty should prevail; moral distress concerns being blocked from acting on one

rationales.whyCorrect: The two concepts differ in where the difficulty sits: a dilemma is a problem of moral judgment, where legitimate duties compete, while moral distress is a problem of moral agency, where the ability to act is constrained. The distinction drives the intervention, since dilemmas are addressed through deliberation, ethics consultation, and stakeholder dialogue, whereas moral distress is addressed by identifying and removing the constraint. Both are experienced by individuals within institutional contexts, and both carry significant emotional consequences, so neither emotional impact nor timing distinguishes them.
rationales.eli10: Both feel like being stuck, which is why students blur them, but they are stuck in different places. In a dilemma the difficulty is upstream, at the judgment: you have not yet settled which obligation should win, because more than one has a real claim. In moral distress the judgment is already made or at least in progress, and the difficulty is downstream, at the doing. That difference tells you where to push. Talking a dilemma through with the right people can genuinely resolve it. Talking through moral distress may help you endure it, but nothing changes until the thing blocking you does.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a healthcare ethics committee or clinical ethics consultation service?

options.text: To offer a structured multidisciplinary forum for clarifying values, improving communication, and recommending options
To investigate staff misconduct and recommend discipline or referral to the licensing board
To issue binding rulings that legally settle disputes between families and the healthcare team
To decide which patients receive scarce treatments when demand for them exceeds available supply

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a nurse repeatedly experiences unresolved moral distress over months of practice?

options.text: Tolerance develops, so comparable situations reliably generate less ethical concern as time goes on

The nurse's personal values are gradually replaced by the values the institution has formally adopted

The documented consequences include disengagement, withdrawal from bedside practice, and reduced willingness to speak up when the next concern arises. Recognizing that the baseline rises rather than falls is the rationale for early ethics consultation, structured debriefing, and changes to the underlying constraint, instead of expecting individuals to absorb repeated compromise.

The next situation therefore does not start from zero; it lands on top of everything still unsettled, so the reaction climbs rather than flattens. That rising curve is the crescendo effect, and it explains a pattern that otherwise looks strange: the nurses who care most about doing right are often the ones who leave.

options.text: Routing ethical concerns through the annual anonymous employee engagement survey for later review

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates a genuine ethical dilemma rather than a clinical, legal, or communication problem?

options.text: The team cannot tell whether a patient's new confusion reflects an infection or a recently started medication

Principles are weighed in context rather than ordered in a fixed hierarchy, and while liability exposure and clinical authority are real considerations, neither substitutes for ethical analysis.
rationales.eli10: Skipping straight to the options is the most common failure in real ethics discussions, and it is expensive. questions.stem: A nurse holds a longstanding moral objection to participating in a particular elective intervention. Which statement accurately distinguishes conscientious objection from patient abandonment?

options.text: Conscientious objection is defined by institutional policy, while abandonment is defined by the individual nurse's own judgment of the situation
Conscientious objection permits withdrawal at any point, provided the nurse afterward documents the moral reasoning behind the refusal in the record
Conscientious objection applies only to procedures that are legally contested, so any other values-based refusal is classified as abandonment
Conscientious objection is raised in advance so care can be transferred; abandonment is leaving an accepted assignment without arranging that transfer

rationales.whyCorrect: The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses (2025 edition) defines conscientious objection as refusal to participate in a lawfully permitted process within one's scope of practice, and interpretive statement 5.3 affirms that nurses have a right and a duty to act according to their personal and professional values; the expectation is that the objection is disclosed in advance so the patient's care continues uninterrupted. Abandonment is a distinct concept governed principally by state nurse practice acts and employer policy, arising when a nurse unilaterally leaves an assignment already accepted without transferring responsibility. The decisive variables are therefore timing and transfer of care, not the sincerity or strength of the nurse's moral conviction, and conscience-based refusal is directed at participating in a specific intervention rather than at the patient.
rationales.eli10: The same belief, held with the same sincerity, produces either a protected professional act or a licensure problem depending on two variables that have nothing to do with the belief itself. The first is timing: an objection raised before you accept responsibility can be planned around, while one raised after leaves a gap in real time. The second is transfer: someone competent must be holding the patient's care when you step back. Note also what conscientious objection is aimed at. It is a refusal to participate in a specific intervention, not a refusal to care for a particular person, and refusing the person moves into discrimination rather than conscience.

questions.stem: An organizational policy appears to conflict with the action a nurse believes is ethically required for a patient. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship among law, organizational policy, and ethical obligation?

options.text: Organizational policy carries the force of statute, so a conflicting ethical judgment must yield to the written policy
Ethical obligations are personal opinions, so policy should govern whenever policy and ethics appear to conflict
Following policy does not by itself make practice ethical, so the nurse acts lawfully while raising the conflict formally
A nurse who judges a policy unethical may set it aside independently, because moral agency outranks institutional rules

rationales.whyCorrect: Interpretive statement 5.3 of the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses (2025 edition) states directly that acting with integrity is not the same as following rules, carrying out orders, or adhering to laws and policies without moral discernment, and it obligates nurses to express concern individually or collectively when integrity is compromised by patterns of institutional behavior. At the same time, unilaterally disregarding policy bypasses the deliberation a genuine dilemma requires, can expose the patient to additional risk, and forfeits the very mechanisms that could change the policy for the next patient. The defensible path uses ethics consultation, the chain of command, and policy-review processes, which is why organizations are expected to maintain those channels.
rationales.eli10: Law, organizational policy, and ethics are three separate systems that usually converge, and the interesting work begins where they do not. Two opposite errors are tempting. The first treats the policy manual as if it settled the ethics, which the ANA Code rejects explicitly: compliance without discernment is not integrity. The second treats private moral conviction as a license to override the rule quietly, which fails for a practical reason as much as a professional one. A policy worked around in silence stays in force and harms the next patient, while a policy formally challenged through consultation, chain of command, or review can actually be rewritten.
